ECE 6390 / RF links

Spreading and capture

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows the geometric reason a distant receiver captures less power even when the medium absorbs none.

Power spreads across a growing spherical surface. In a chosen far-field direction, flux density is S = PtGt/(4πR²), where Pt is accepted transmit power in watts, Gt is dimensionless gain and R is range in metres. EIRP = PtGt is the isotropic power that would produce the same flux in that direction.

The receiver captures flux through its effective aperture Ae, giving Pr = S Ae. For a reciprocal antenna, Ae = Gr λ²/(4π), with wavelength λ in metres. Combining these expressions gives Friis transmission. Free-space path loss is the ratio (4πR/λ)², commonly expressed in dB.

Changing frequency at fixed receive gain changes effective aperture. Changing frequency at fixed physical aperture can change receive gain instead. State what is held fixed before interpreting the frequency dependence.

Example

Doubling range spreads the same radiated power over four times the area. Received power falls by a factor of four, or 6.02 dB, when gains and wavelength are fixed.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. If range increases by a factor of ten with all antenna gains fixed, how many dB does received power change?

    Pr is proportional to R⁻².

    Received power falls by 20 dB: 10 log₁₀(1/100) = −20 dB.

    2. At fixed receive gain, why does a shorter wavelength reduce effective aperture?

    Use Ae = Gr λ²/(4π).

    Effective aperture scales as λ² at fixed dimensionless gain. A given flux therefore delivers less power. A fixed physical antenna need not maintain the same gain as frequency changes.
